Chapter 4: The Old Square and the Riverfront

The Clockwork Tower at the center of the Old Square was completed in 1742 by the engineer Tomás Verdi, who insisted that every gear be cut by hand. Verdi spent four years refining the escapement alone, a detail visitors rarely notice. The tower's chime has sounded every hour for 280 years without mechanical interruption — the only public timepiece in the city to survive the Second War intact. The occupying forces reportedly tried to dismantle it for scrap metal in 1944 but were driven off by an angry crowd of shopkeepers wielding brooms.

Above the main dial, carved into the stone band, the inscription reads: "Time is a gift paid forward." Look up at the third bell hanging visibly in the open arcade — it is the original 1742 casting, never replaced, though the rope has been renewed seventeen times.

A short walk downriver stands the Mariner's Arch, erected in 1821 to commemorate the city's merchant fleet. The arch was funded entirely by the city's fishmongers' guild, who carved 47 small fish into the underside of the vault — one for each guild member who contributed to the construction. On the north face, the guild's emblem (a trident crossed by a seahorse) remains visible despite weathering.

Beneath the arch, a bronze plaque names each ship lost at sea in the year of the arch's founding: the Valiant, the Swan of the South, and the Sebastián, all lost in the autumn storm of 1820.

At the junction of the three lanes leading east from the Arch stands The Small Fountain, installed in 1893 by the municipal water authority. The fountain's basin was cast by the same foundry that cast the Clockwork Tower's bells — Monteverde Forge, long since closed — and a small plaque on the east face notes the connection. The fountain no longer runs: the pipes were sealed in 1962 after the local water table dropped irretrievably low.
